provenance: Original fictional conversations, reviews, and files created for this simulation; not recovered CompuServe archives.

messages.author: Harbor64
messages.subject: DOCK64: can you land with fuel left?
messages.body: I have uploaded DOCK64.BAS, a short numeric docking game for the C64. You begin 30 units above the pad with 30 fuel units. Each turn you choose thrust from zero through five. The display reports altitude, downward speed, and fuel. A landing faster than two units per turn is a crash. There are no machine-code routines or disk writes; the entire game is a BASIC listing.

messages.author: Petunia
messages.subject: RE: DOCK64: can you land with fuel left?
messages.body: First attempt: I spent all my fuel holding position and then fell! The useful clue is that gravity adds two to downward speed each turn. Thrust three reduces that speed by one. I started with thrust two for four turns, then tried three and coasted the final short distance. Keep a paper log of the numbers; it is much easier to understand the second flight.

messages.author: Harbor64
messages.subject: RE: DOCK64: can you land with fuel left?
messages.body: Version 1.1 rejects fractional thrust and values outside zero through five, and limits thrust to the fuel still aboard. The listing is ordinary text, not a tokenized C64 program. Type the numbered lines into BASIC, or use your emulator's text-paste facility, then RUN. C64NOTES.TXT explains that distinction. Post your landing speed and fuel remaining so we can compare flights.

messages.author: WorkbenchWren
messages.subject: A repeatable test beats a drawer full of guesses
messages.body: I keep forgetting which disk I used when a drawing program behaved correctly. My new AMIGALOG.TXT worksheet records the machine, memory, Workbench disk label, application version, extra utilities, and exact steps. I start from the same disk and change one item per run. It is slower than declaring the expansion board guilty, but my notes finally mean something.

messages.author: CopperCat
messages.subject: RE: A repeatable test beats a drawer full of guesses
messages.body: Please include the expected result as well as the observed one. My report said "the picture is wrong," which told the author almost nothing. The useful report was "load the small sample, select the second palette, save under a new name, reopen; the first two colors exchange places." I kept the original drawing untouched and sent the author a copy of the small sample.

messages.author: WorkbenchWren
messages.subject: RE: A repeatable test beats a drawer full of guesses
messages.body: Added fields for expected result, actual result, and whether the problem repeats after a fresh start. There is also space for the name of a backup copy. The worksheet contains no commands and changes no settings. Print it or fill it in with a text editor. Next club night I want us to bring one complete report apiece instead of a bag of unlabeled disks.

messages.author: CopperCat
messages.subject: December postcard exchange: plain characters only
messages.body: PIXELCAT.TXT is my entry for the club postcard exchange: a cat watching a tiny terminal, with a note about keeping each line short. I used ordinary printable characters so the design can travel between our machines. It is deliberately not PETSCII art. Please open it with a fixed-width font and leave the spaces alone.

messages.author: Petunia
messages.subject: RE: December postcard exchange: plain characters only
messages.body: The first copy looked like a collapsed tent because my editor replaced several spaces with a tab. A plain-text copy fixed it. Our exchange rules should be a maximum of 38 columns, no cursor-control sequences, and no dependence on color. That gives the 40-column crowd room to read without horizontal scrolling.

messages.author: Harbor64
messages.subject: RE: December postcard exchange: plain characters only
messages.body: Let us make the next theme "my computer after midnight." Include your handle in the file, but no mailing address. If you adapt the cat, say what you changed. I will collect entries as separate text files so nobody has to extract an unfamiliar archive simply to read a greeting.

messages.author: OrchardAnn
messages.subject: ORCHARD: a basket-counting type-in for club night
messages.body: ORCHARD.BAS gives five rounds of multiplication practice. Each round shows a number of baskets and the apples in each basket. Enter the total; the program keeps your score and shows the right answer after a miss. I used a fixed sequence of problems so a parent can work through the same sheet beside a child. It is an original Applesoft type-in, not a commercial disk.

messages.author: AppleTutor
messages.subject: RE: ORCHARD: a basket-counting type-in for club night
messages.body: This is a good place to demonstrate variables. B holds baskets, A holds apples per basket, and C holds correct answers. Before RUN, use LIST and find the line that compares the answer with A*B. For a younger player, lower the numbers in the two assignment lines. Keep the original listing so the exercise can always be restored.

messages.author: OrchardAnn
messages.subject: RE: ORCHARD: a basket-counting type-in for club night
messages.body: The file includes numbered REM lines identifying the program. Begin with an empty BASIC program and enter the listing exactly; APPLETIP.TXT includes a short checklist. Version 1.1 shows the expected answer after an incorrect response. My club test sheet uses answers 6, 12, 20, 30, and 42. Please mention the version when posting a result.

messages.author: DiskDaisy
messages.subject: What belongs on a disk catalog card?
messages.body: My club disks have labels such as "STUFF" and "MORE STUFF." DISKLOG.TXT is an attempt to retire those names. It has fields for a volume label, date, disk format as reported by the software, program names, and the location of a backup. It also has a separate printer-test log; yesterday's good printout is now clipped to the correct entry.

messages.author: AppleTutor
messages.subject: RE: What belongs on a disk catalog card?
messages.body: Record whether a disk is your master, a working copy, or a disk received from someone else. Do not assume two disks with similar labels contain the same version. I also write down which program created a document, because a filename by itself does not explain how to open it. The catalog should describe what you actually checked.

messages.author: DiskDaisy
messages.subject: RE: What belongs on a disk catalog card?
messages.body: I added a "last checked" line and a place for the application version. Nothing in this form formats or copies a disk. It is a printable worksheet. My next experiment is to catalog ten disks at a time rather than trying to reorganize the entire shelf in one evening.

messages.author: OrchardAnn
messages.subject: A welcome screen for the next user-group meeting
messages.body: APPLEART.TXT is a small welcome card for the December meeting. It fits within 38 columns and uses printable ASCII only. We can show it in a terminal capture or print it at the top of the club handout. The title is fictional, so replace it with your own club's name if you use it.

messages.author: DiskDaisy
messages.subject: RE: A welcome screen for the next user-group meeting
messages.body: I would put the meeting agenda below the picture: introductions, one type-in demonstration, a disk-labeling workshop, and questions. Four short items are easier to read than a screen full of rules. We should also leave a space on the printed copy for the next meeting date.

messages.author: AppleTutor
messages.subject: RE: A welcome screen for the next user-group meeting
messages.body: For the type-in demonstration, use ORCHARD.BAS and invite someone to predict the next pair of numbers before pressing Return. Then show the relevant lines with LIST. The picture makes a friendly opening, but the tiny program gives everyone something they can change and understand.

messages.author: GemGwen
messages.subject: A project folder that the next editor can understand
messages.body: Our club newsletter arrived on three disks with no explanation of which file was final. STDESK.TXT proposes a simple project checklist: original text, working copy, finished copy, a list of assets, and the application version used. The names are suggestions, not a utility that moves files. I want another member to be able to continue the issue without a telephone interrogation.

messages.author: MidiMoth
messages.subject: RE: A project folder that the next editor can understand
messages.body: Add the page size and font names to the handover note. A file can open successfully and still produce a different page count. Keep an example printout with the project and note which printer produced it. If a font or image is not included, say so explicitly instead of letting the next editor search every disk.

messages.author: GemGwen
messages.subject: RE: A project folder that the next editor can understand
messages.body: The revised checklist has a handover section and a box for missing assets. It also asks for a plain-text copy of the article text. That is useful when two club members have different publishing programs. STCLUB.TXT is our small sample issue, and it can be read without installing any publishing software.

messages.author: MidiMoth
messages.subject: TEMPO.BAS: quarter-note timing on paper
messages.body: TEMPO.BAS converts beats per minute to the duration of a quarter note in milliseconds and to the length of a four-beat bar in seconds. It is a calculator for ST BASIC, not a MIDI driver or a metronome. At 120 BPM I expect 500 milliseconds per quarter note and two seconds per bar. Enter zero to finish.

messages.author: ClockworkST
messages.subject: RE: TEMPO.BAS: quarter-note timing on paper
messages.body: I tried 60 and 120 first because the answers are easy to check. The display rounds the note duration to one decimal place and the bar duration to two. Remember that the bar calculation assumes four quarter-note beats; it does not infer a time signature from a song name. I would put that assumption directly on the opening screen.

messages.author: MidiMoth
messages.subject: RE: TEMPO.BAS: quarter-note timing on paper
messages.body: Done in 1.1. The program accepts whole BPM values from 20 through 300 and prints the assumption before asking for input. MIDIPLAN.TXT is a separate rehearsal worksheet for instrument names, channels, patch notes, and cable labels. Neither file sends any MIDI messages or changes an instrument.

messages.author: GemGwen
messages.subject: The ST club newsletter needs small, reproducible projects
messages.body: The sample STCLUB.TXT issue contains a short editor's note, a tempo-calculator exercise, and a project handover checklist. I would rather run one listing that members can understand than promise a large application we never finish. Suggested next issue: bring a one-page account of something you learned while preparing a document or a rehearsal.

messages.author: ClockworkST
messages.subject: RE: The ST club newsletter needs small, reproducible projects
messages.body: A useful submission should include the starting conditions, steps, expected result, and what happened. For a calculator, give two or three inputs with known answers. For a picture or document, include a plain-text explanation of the intended layout. That lets other members distinguish a program error from a missing font or a different setting.

messages.author: MidiMoth
messages.subject: RE: The ST club newsletter needs small, reproducible projects
messages.body: I volunteer the timing examples: 60 BPM gives 1000 milliseconds and four seconds per four-beat bar; 120 gives 500 and two. The next question is how to explain rounding without making a musician read a mathematics chapter. Keep it short enough to download before the kettle boils.

messages.author: PathPilot
messages.subject: A startup notebook before changing CONFIG.SYS
messages.body: DOSNOTES.TXT is a notebook-style guide to recording a working setup. It explains what PATH and PROMPT do and includes a small example, but it does not install anything. I begin by writing down the DOS version, available memory as reported by my tools, and the programs I need for the task. Then I keep a copy of the original startup files before making one documented change.

messages.author: BatchBeth
messages.subject: RE: A startup notebook before changing CONFIG.SYS
messages.body: Please separate commands typed at the prompt from lines intended for a startup file. That distinction caused most of the confusion at our last club meeting. Your PATH example should also say that its directories must already exist. A path entry does not install the program or create a directory.

messages.author: PathPilot
messages.subject: RE: A startup notebook before changing CONFIG.SYS
messages.body: The guide now labels the examples and explains that PATH replaces the search list when assigned a value. It does not tell members to overwrite their own startup files. My main suggestion is still to record the before-and-after result. A shorter startup file is not an improvement if it omits a driver your application needs.

messages.author: SectorSam
messages.subject: LOSTDISK: a complete tiny adventure in BASIC
messages.body: LOSTDISK.BAS is a small text adventure for GW-BASIC. Search the club room, find a key, open the cabinet, and return the missing demo disk. The commands are numbers so there are no spelling puzzles. It uses no external data files, and it neither reads nor writes your disks. The puzzle state lives in variables until the program ends.

messages.author: BatchBeth
messages.subject: RE: LOSTDISK: a complete tiny adventure in BASIC
messages.body: I tried the cabinet before finding the key and received the locked message, then used the desk and returned to the cabinet. That path works. I also tried returning a disk before collecting it. The program correctly kept me in the room. Five menu options are enough for this exercise; a larger parser would hide the state changes we want beginners to see.

messages.author: SectorSam
messages.subject: RE: LOSTDISK: a complete tiny adventure in BASIC
messages.body: Version 1.1 accepts only whole-number choices from one through five. Please read the REM lines and try adding a second object as a club exercise. The companion CALLCOST.BAS estimates a fictional session cost from minutes and an hourly rate; at 30 minutes and 12 dollars per hour the answer is six dollars. Neither program interacts with the simulator's account balance.

messages.author: BatchBeth
messages.subject: CLUBLIST: a text roster with useful blanks
messages.body: CLUBLIST.TXT contains fictional example entries and a blank record form for a computer club. Each record has a handle, computer, interests, current project, and preferred forum. There are no telephone numbers or home addresses. The file is plain text so it remains readable without a particular database package.

messages.author: PathPilot
messages.subject: RE: CLUBLIST: a text roster with useful blanks
messages.body: I like the project field. "Interested in modems" is vague, while "writing down a repeatable connection test" gives someone a reason to reply. Include a last-updated date so an old request does not look like a current emergency. For a real roster, let members choose what they want included.

messages.author: SectorSam
messages.subject: RE: CLUBLIST: a text roster with useful blanks
messages.body: My example entry points to LOSTDISK.BAS and asks for a different solution path. That connects the roster to something in the library. Next meeting we can pair a first-time programmer with someone who has already typed the listing, and exchange notes through the forum instead of adding everyone to a mailing list.

files.description: A fuel-limited landing game with numeric controls.
files.instructions: ASCII source listing, not a tokenized disk image. Enter numbered lines in the named BASIC interpreter, then RUN. Programs are original simulation content.
history: 1.1: Validate whole-number thrust and limit it to remaining fuel.

reviews.author: Petunia
reviews.text: The displayed fuel makes every choice matter. Text type-in, not a ready-to-load C64 disk file.

files.content:
10 REM DOCK64 1.1 - ORIGINAL CLUB TYPE-IN
20 H=30:V=3:F=30
30 PRINT "DOCK64 - LAND AT SPEED 2 OR LESS"
40 PRINT "DOWNWARD SPEED IS POSITIVE"
50 PRINT "HEIGHT";H;" SPEED";V
60 PRINT "FUEL";F
70 INPUT "THRUST 0 TO 5";T
80 IF T<0 OR T>5 OR T<>INT(T) THEN 70
90 IF T>F THEN T=F
100 F=F-T:V=V+2-T:H=H-V
110 IF H>0 THEN 50
120 IF V>2 THEN 150
130 PRINT "SAFE LANDING! FUEL LEFT";F
140 END
150 PRINT "CRASH - LANDING SPEED";V
160 END

files.name: C64NOTES.TXT
files.description: A short guide to entering and checking BASIC listings.
files.system: C64 BASIC V2; readable on any text terminal
files.instructions: Open in a plain-text editor or print with a fixed-width font. Original simulation content; no installation needed.

reviews.author: Harbor64
reviews.text: The distinction between ASCII listings and PRG files saves beginners a confusing LOAD attempt.

files.content:
C64 TYPE-IN DESK - ORIGINAL CLUB NOTES

A text listing and a saved BASIC program are different things. The .BAS
files in this collection contain printable numbered lines. They are not
tokenized PRG files and are not disk images. Start with an empty BASIC
program, enter the lines, and use LIST to inspect the result before RUN.
An emulator may offer a text-paste facility; consult its instructions.

Each line number identifies a line. Entering a replacement with the same
number replaces that line. Keep a copy of the original listing before
experimenting. DOCK64 uses PRINT for display, INPUT for a number, and
IF ... THEN to select a branch. A colon separates statements on one line.

DOCK64 CHECK FLIGHT
Enter thrust 2 four times: heights 27, 24, 21, 18; speed stays 3.
Then enter 3: height 16, speed 2. Enter 2 eight times to land gently.
The ending should report 3 fuel and a safe landing at speed 2.
Try a different sequence and record height, speed, and fuel each turn.

The listing uses no graphics, sound, device access, POKE, or machine code.
Reference: Commodore 64 Programmer's Reference Guide, BASIC chapters.
https://www.commodore.ca/manuals/c64_programmers_reference/c64-programmers_reference.htm
These are newly written notes, not a transcription of the manual.

files.name: ORCHARD.BAS
files.description: Five rounds of basket-and-apple arithmetic practice.
files.instructions: ASCII source listing, not a tokenized disk image. Enter numbered lines in the named BASIC interpreter, then RUN. Programs are original simulation content.
history: 1.1: Show the correct total after a miss.

reviews.author: AppleTutor
reviews.text: Known answers make this a useful first type-in and a simple variables lesson.

files.content:
10 REM ORCHARD 1.1 - ORIGINAL TYPE-IN
20 C=0
30 PRINT "ORCHARD - FIVE COUNTING ROUNDS"
40 FOR R=1 TO 5
50 B=R+1:A=R+2
60 PRINT "BASKETS: ";B
70 PRINT "APPLES IN EACH: ";A
80 INPUT "TOTAL APPLES";N
90 IF N=A*B THEN 120
100 PRINT "THE TOTAL IS ";A*B
110 GOTO 140
120 PRINT "CORRECT!"
130 C=C+1
140 NEXT R
150 PRINT "CORRECT ANSWERS: ";C;" OF 5"
160 END

files.name: APPLETIP.TXT
files.description: Applesoft type-in checklist and ORCHARD exercises.
files.instructions: Open in a plain-text editor or print with a fixed-width font. Original simulation content; no installation needed.

reviews.author: OrchardAnn
reviews.text: A short lesson that can be printed beside the computer.

files.content:
APPLESOFT TYPE-IN CHECKLIST
Original Apple II Forum workshop sheet.

1. Keep your existing work before starting an empty BASIC program.
2. Enter each numbered line of ORCHARD.BAS exactly as shown.
3. LIST the program. Check line numbers, quotation marks, and punctuation.
4. RUN. The five expected totals are 6, 12, 20, 30, and 42.
5. An all-correct run reports 5 OF 5. Five zero answers report 0 OF 5.

The downloadable .BAS file is an ASCII listing. It is not a tokenized
Applesoft program or a bootable Apple disk. Use a text-paste feature only
if your emulator supports it; otherwise type the numbered lines.

READING THE PROGRAM
R is the round. B is baskets. A is apples per basket. N is the answer.
C counts correct answers. FOR and NEXT repeat the rounds. IF tests the
answer, and GOTO skips the success message after a wrong answer.

EXERCISES
Change line 50 so every basket contains two apples.
Write down all five expected answers before running the changed version.
Change the opening message. Keep the double quotes around the text.
Restore the original listing and verify the original five answers again.

The program performs no disk operations and uses no graphics commands.
Reference: Apple's Applesoft BASIC programming manuals; these notes and
the exercise are original simulation material, not archived forum posts.

reviews.author: ClockworkST
reviews.text: Short enough to read in one sitting and tied to files actually in this library.

files.content:
THE SMALL SCREEN - DECEMBER 1988
An original fictional Atari ST club newsletter.

FROM THE EDITOR
This month's rule is simple: bring a project another member can finish.
A folder full of unexplained files is a puzzle, not a handover. Include a
short note, the application version, and an example of the intended result.

WORKSHOP: TIME ON PAPER
Our TEMPO.BAS type-in answers two questions: how long is one quarter note,
and how long is a bar containing four of them? At 120 BPM the answers are
500 milliseconds and two seconds. Try 60 BPM, then explain why both
durations doubled. The program does not operate your instruments.

DESKTOP DESK
The next editor may not own your fonts. STDESK.TXT asks you to identify
missing assets and include plain article text. A printout can explain a
layout more quickly than three telephone calls about the second column.

NEXT MEETING
Bring one short project, a known result, and a question. We will pair
members and see whether each can reproduce the other's result from notes.
No prize for the largest pile of disks; applause for the clearest notes.

100 PRINT "ESTIMATED DOLLARS: ";C

130 END

reviews.author: BatchBeth
reviews.text: Try the locked cabinet first. Then inspect the desk, revisit the cabinet, and return the disk.

files.content:
10 REM LOSTDISK 1.1 - ORIGINAL ADVENTURE
20 K=0:D=0
30 PRINT "THE CLUB DEMO DISK IS MISSING."
40 PRINT "1 DESK  2 CABINET  3 NOTICE"
50 PRINT "4 RETURN DISK  5 QUIT"
60 INPUT "CHOICE";C
70 IF C<1 OR C>5 OR C<>INT(C) THEN 60
80 ON C GOTO 100,140,200,230,290
100 PRINT "A BRASS KEY IS UNDER THE NOTES."
110 K=1
120 GOTO 40
140 IF K=0 THEN 180
150 PRINT "THE KEY FITS. YOU TAKE THE DISK."
160 D=1
170 GOTO 40
180 PRINT "THE CABINET IS LOCKED."
190 GOTO 40
200 PRINT "NOTICE: THE DEMO STARTS AT EIGHT."
210 PRINT "PLEASE RETURN THE CLUB DISK."
220 GOTO 40
230 IF D=0 THEN 270
240 PRINT "YOU RETURN THE DISK. SHOW SAVED!"
250 END
270 PRINT "YOU DO NOT HAVE THE DISK YET."
280 GOTO 40
290 PRINT "YOU LEAVE THE CLUB ROOM."
300 END

files.instructions: Open in a plain-text editor or print with a fixed-width font. Original simulation content; no installation needed.
history: 1.1: Added explicit ASCII LOAD and program checks.

reviews.author: BatchBeth
reviews.text: The examples are separated from the blank notebook, so they are harder to mistake for an installer.

files.content:
DOS WORKSHOP NOTEBOOK
Original notes, not an automatic setup script.

RECORD FIRST
DOS version:
Application and version:
Current startup-file backup location:
Available memory as reported by your tools:
Driver or resident programs required for this task:
One proposed change and expected result:

EXAMPLES TYPED AT A DOS PROMPT
PROMPT $P$G
  Displays the current drive and directory followed by >.
PATH C:\DOS;C:\UTIL
  Example search list only. These directories must already exist and
  contain your programs. Assigning PATH replaces its existing search
  list; it does not create directories or install software.

Keep a working copy of your own startup files before editing them. Make
one change, record the result, and retain the configuration your required
applications need. These notes do not supply a replacement CONFIG.SYS.

GW-BASIC FILES
CALLCOST.BAS and LOSTDISK.BAS are ASCII source. From GW-BASIC in the
directory containing a listing, use LOAD "LOSTDISK.BAS" and then RUN.
LOAD replaces the program currently in memory, so save your work first.
The examples do not access files or change the simulator account.

CALLCOST CHECK: 30 minutes at 12 per hour is 6 dollars. Zero minutes ends.
LOSTDISK CHECK: choices 1, 2, 4 solve the puzzle; choice 5 quits.
